newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian PM may lose influence under govt reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Russian PM may lose influence under govt reshuffle.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin risks being undermined by government changes unveiled on Monday, despite last-minute efforts to protect his own position in a battle for influence.

Chernomyrdin announced the top eight ministers below him in the cabinet after hard bargaining with President Boris Yeltsin and new First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, which ended in clear gains for the latter and for liberal reformers.

Chernomyrdin, 58, remains a potential successor to Yeltsin when his presidential term ends in 2000. The final balance of forces in the cabinet will not be clear until the names of the lower-ranking ministers are announced.

But the promotion of several Chubais proteges and the surprise appointment of potential presidential hopeful Boris Nemtsov to the powerful role of a first deputy premier do not augur well for the stolid, 58-year-old prime minister.

"Cheromyrdin risks becoming a lame duck in the new cabinet and he could be limited to having little more than a status as a figurehead," said Andrei Kortunov, head of the Russian Science Foundation think-tank. "It looks like a net loss for him".

Yeltsin, 66, has used the cabinet reshuffle to try to reassert his authority after months of illness and appointed Chubais, 41, as a first deputy prime minister on March 7 to inject new life into stalled economic reforms.

Chubais and Chernomyrdin are both pro-reform and are united in their support for Yeltsin. They worked well together during the eight months Yeltsin was out of the Kremlin, largely running the country together.
They could eventually be a presidential election team, with Chubais -- who is widely unpopular but a brilliant organiser -- backing the candidacy of Chernomyrdin.

But Chubais's carte blanche in tackling economic reforms has taken away some of Chernomyrdin's responsibilities and his dual appointment as finance minister is a further sign of the former Kremlin aide's stature and influence.
New deputy prime ministers Alfred Kokh and Yakov Urinson are also like-minded liberal reformers who could fall more under Chubais's wing than Chernomyrdin's.

Chernomyrdin's rearguard action to limit the number of liberal reformers in the cabinet to maintain his own influence and a delicate balance between reformers and more conservative groups appears to have failed.

"The reshuffle has moved a critical mass in favour of the supporters of reform and creates a like-minded economic team in which Chernomyrdin looks superfluous," said Sergei Markov of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace think-tank.
Nemtsov's appointment to the same rank as Chubais as a first deputy prime minister is also a double-edged sword.

Yeltsin had said last week that Chubais would be the only first deputy premier, meaning Nemtsov's appointment could be seen as a blow to Chubais's prestige and a gesture to Chernomyrdin's concerns at the former Kremlin aide's growing powers.

But it also serves as a warning to Chernomyrdin that the dynamic 37-year-old regional governor could emerge as Yeltsin's chosen successor and reminds the prime minister that the president is back at the helm and in control of appointments.
Despite this, the changes need not be seen as fatal for Chernomyrdin, who has been overseeing reforms as prime minister since December 1992 and has proved to be a great survivor.
"It is clear Chernomyrdin fought a battle of sorts over the appointments but it was nevertheless not a battle of enemies. It was more a strategic battle between allies," Markov said.
Some political analysts say Chernomyrdin remains the most obvious choice of the ruling elite to replace Yeltsin, even if he lacks charisma and would be hard to elect.
"We must look at the other cabinet changes for signs of exactly what influence Chernomyrdin retains," a diplomat with long experience in Russia said.

"If Chubais fails, he could be made a scapegoat instead of Chernomyrdin. Chernomyrdin also has a chance now to be freed from some of his duties to brush up his image, take some lessons in public speaking and become a better presidential candidate."
